p: The Hebrew lists the names alone. The Greek adds "the sons of Noah," making clear the last three are brothers.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
Greek (Codex Vaticanus and most Greek manuscripts, as reported in commentaries); NIV, BSB
readings.orig: Νωε· υἱοὶ Νωε· Σημ, Χαμ, Ιαφεθ
readings.en: Noah. The sons of Noah: Shem, Ham and Japheth
readings.plain: the sons of Noah: Shem, Ham and Japheth

why: The Greek reading is almost certainly a helpful addition, explaining what the Hebrew leaves to the reader who knows Genesis 5:32. The shorter Hebrew is the harder reading and fits the bare style of 1:1–4.
b: A note on the Greek of Chronicles: the Greek translation, called Paraleipomena ("things left out"), was made in Egypt, probably in the 100s BC. Codex Vaticanus (300s AD) is generally a good witness to the Old Greek of Chronicles; Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD) and the Lucianic manuscripts were often corrected toward the Hebrew. In these chapters the translators frequently misread or respelled names, so a Greek name that differs from the Hebrew is usually a slip, not a better reading. The cases given here are those where the Greek may preserve something real.

p: The Leningrad Codex reads Diphath. Other witnesses read Riphath, as Genesis 10:3 does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
Many Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek and the Latin Vulgate, as reported in commentaries; Genesis 10:3; NIV, BSB

why: The letters dalet and resh are nearly identical, and Riphath is surely the original name, as Genesis shows. The Plain English Translation prints the Leningrad Codex as it stands, as it does with other spelling differences, and the note explains.

p: The Hebrew makes Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech sons of Shem. Genesis 10:23 makes them sons of Aram.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: and Aram and Uz and Hul and Gether and Meshech

readings.w: One Hebrew manuscript and Codex Alexandrinus (Greek), as reported in commentaries, and Genesis 10:23; NIV, BSB
readings.en: and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz
readings.plain: Lud and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz

why: Genesis 10:23 reads "Aram's sons were Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash." The words "the sons of Aram" probably dropped out of Chronicles when a scribe's eye skipped from one "Aram" to the next. But the Chronicler also shortens Genesis throughout these lists, and the Hebrew as it stands is what the Masoretes handed on, so the Plain English Translation keeps it and the note on Meshech explains. Codex Vaticanus lacks 1:11–16 and 1:17b–23 altogether, probably also by skipping.

p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) has Aliah; the reading tradition (Qere) and Genesis 36:40 have Alvah.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); Genesis 36:40; NIV, ESV, BSB
Ketiv (the written consonants); KJV

why: The letters waw and yod are often confused. The Qere agrees with Genesis 36:40, so the Plain English Translation follows it. On Ketiv and Qere, see the note on 1:46.

p: The Hebrew here reads Dara. Many Hebrew manuscripts, the Syriac and the Targum read Darda, as in 1 Kings 4:31.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
Many Hebrew manuscripts, the Syriac and the Targum, as reported in commentaries; 1 Kings 4:31; the Greek has Darad; NIV

why: The two forms differ by one repeated letter. If these are the wise men of 1 Kings 4:31, Darda is probably original. The Plain English Translation keeps the Leningrad spelling and notes the link.

a: After Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah, Hezron's wife Abijah
p: The Hebrew has Hezron die "in Caleb-ephrathah." The Greek and Latin say Caleb went in to Ephrathah after Hezron died.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, BSB
readings.orig: וְאַחַר מוֹת־חֶצְרוֹן בְּכָלֵב אֶפְרָתָה וְאֵשֶׁת חֶצְרוֹן אֲבִיָּה
readings.en: after Hezron's death in Caleb-ephrathah, and Hezron's wife Abijah
readings.plain: After Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah, Hezron's wife Abijah

readings.w: Greek (Brenton's text) and Latin Vulgate
readings.orig: μετὰ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν Εσερων ἦλθεν Χαλεβ εἰς Εφραθα· καὶ ἡ γυνὴ Εσερων Αβια
readings.en: after Hezron died, Caleb came to Ephrathah; and Hezron's wife was Abia
readings.plain: After Hezron died, Caleb went in to Ephrathah. Hezron's wife Abijah

readings.w: A modern conjecture, not found in any manuscript or ancient version; ESV, NRSV
readings.orig: בָּא כָלֵב אֶפְרָתָה וְאֵשֶׁת חֶצְרוֹן אָבִיו
readings.en: Caleb went in to Ephrathah, the wife of Hezron his father
readings.plain: After Hezron died, Caleb went in to Ephrathah, his father Hezron's wife

why: The Greek and Latin read ba Khalev, "Caleb came," for be-Khalev, "in Caleb," and keep Abijah as the name of Hezron's wife. That fits 2:19 and 2:50, where Ephrathah is Caleb's wife. Some modern scholars go further and read aviv, "his father," for aviyyah, "Abijah," so that Caleb marries his father's widow, a way of claiming a father's place (compare 5:1), though the law forbids it (Leviticus 18:8). That second change has no ancient witness. A place called Caleb-ephrathah is otherwise unknown, though 1 Samuel 30:14 knows a "Negev of Caleb." The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text.

p: The Hebrew calls Solomon's mother Bath-shua. The Greek, the Latin and 2 Samuel 11:3 have Bathsheba.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
One Hebrew manuscript (as reported in commentaries), the Greek (Bersabee), the Latin Vulgate (Bethsabee) and 2 Samuel 11:3; NIV, BSB

why: Shua and sheba may be two forms of one name, or the letters may have been confused. The Masoretic form matters because it is the same Hebrew as Judah's Canaanite wife in 2:3, "Shua's daughter" (bat-shua), so the mothers of Judah's first sons and of Solomon share a name. The Greek and Latin likely made the name agree with Samuel. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text.

t: Was Zerubbabel the son of Pedaiah or of Shealtiel?
p: The Hebrew calls Zerubbabel Pedaiah's son. The Greek calls him Shealtiel's son, as Ezra, Haggai and Matthew do.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei

readings.w: Greek (Rahlfs' printed text; the Greek manuscripts are divided, and some read Pedaiah)
readings.orig: καὶ υἱοὶ Σαλαθιηλ· Ζοροβαβελ καὶ Σεμεϊ
readings.en: and the sons of Salathiel: Zorobabel and Semei

why: Everywhere else Zerubbabel is "son of Shealtiel" (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1; Matthew 1:12). The Greek probably made Chronicles agree with them. The Hebrew is the harder reading. Some explain it by a levirate marriage: if Shealtiel died childless, his brother Pedaiah could have fathered a son in his name (Deuteronomy 25:5–6); others think "son" in Ezra means heir or grandson. See the topic on Zerubbabel.

a: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah
t: Sons of Hananiah, or a chain of generations?
p: The Hebrew lists four groups of "sons" with no link. The Greek reads "his son" each time, adding four generations.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.orig: בְּנֵי רְפָיָה בְּנֵי אַרְנָן בְּנֵי עֹבַדְיָה בְּנֵי שְׁכַנְיָה
readings.en: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah
readings.plain: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah

readings.w: Greek, Syriac and Latin Vulgate, as reported in commentaries
readings.orig: Ραφαια υἱὸς αὐτοῦ, Ορνα υἱὸς αὐτοῦ, Αβδια υἱὸς αὐτοῦ, Σεχενια υἱὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah
readings.plain: his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah

why: The Hebrew bene, "sons of," and beno, "his son," differ by one letter. If the Greek is right, David's line runs four generations longer, and the list reaches well into the 300s BC. The Hebrew is hard to explain (who are these four families?), which is one reason some scholars prefer the Greek. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and explains in the note on 3:24.

p: The reading tradition (Qere) has Hodaviah; the written consonants (Ketiv) a longer form that KJV gives as Hodaiah.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); NIV, ESV, BSB
Ketiv (the written consonants); KJV

why: Both forms mean "give thanks to the LORD." The Qere matches the name Hodaviah in 5:24 and 9:7.

a: These belonged to the father of Etam
t: Father of Etam, or sons of Etam?
p: The Hebrew begins "These were the father of Etam," which needs smoothing. The Greek has "the sons of Etam."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and these were the father of Etam
readings.plain: These belonged to the father of Etam

readings.w: Greek, as reported in commentaries; ESV
readings.en: and these were the sons of Etam
readings.plain: These were the sons of Etam

why: The Hebrew is awkward but makes sense if Etam is a town and these are the clans who belonged to its founder (see the note on 2:42). The Greek may have smoothed it. The Plain English Translation adds "belonged to" to make the Hebrew readable.

p: The reading tradition (Qere) has Zohar; the written consonants (Ketiv) have Izhar. KJV blends them as Jezoar.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); NIV, ESV, BSB
Ketiv (the written consonants)
KJV (Ketiv consonants read with Qere vowels)

why: Ketiv and Qere differ by one letter, waw ("and") or yod. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as it does throughout.

t: Hathath alone, or Hathath and Meonothai?
p: The Hebrew names one son of Othniel. The Greek and Latin add Meonothai, who begins the next verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: and the sons of Othniel: Hathath

readings.w: Greek (some manuscripts) and Latin Vulgate, as reported in commentaries; NIV, BSB
readings.orig: καὶ υἱοὶ Γοθονιηλ· Αθαθ καὶ Μαωναθι
readings.en: and the sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai
readings.plain: The sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai.

why: Verse 14 opens "Meonothai fathered Ophrah" without introducing him, so a scribe probably skipped one of two "Meonothai"s. The Greek reading is likely original. But it is easy to see where the reader would supply the name, and the Masoretic Text is clear enough, so the Plain English Translation keeps it.

p: The Hebrew says "she conceived" with no subject. The Greek reads "Jether fathered Miriam."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
Greek (Brenton's text)

why: The Greek supplies a subject from the names just listed, making Jether the father of Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah. Most scholars think the Hebrew is the older text and that the missing subject is Bithiah, named at the end of 4:18 (see the note). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew says Simeon went toward Gedor. The Greek says Gerar, a town in the western Negev that fits the story better.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Greek (Codex Vaticanus and others, as reported in commentaries)

why: Gedor is a town in Judah's hill country (Joshua 15:58; 4:4, 18), far from Simeon's land. Gerar, where Abraham and Isaac lived among the Philistines (Genesis 20:1; 26:1), lies in the western Negev, rich in pasture, near "people from Ham" (4:40; 2 Chronicles 14:13–14). The Hebrew letters d and r are easily confused. Many scholars prefer the Greek. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew, since a Gedor in the south is possible, and the note on 4:40 explains.

p: The reading tradition (Qere) has "the sons of Elkanah"; the written consonants (Ketiv) "his son."

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); KJV
Ketiv (the written consonants); NIV, ESV, BSB, which read "Elkanah his son"

why: The Ketiv makes 6:25–26 one continuous line, "Ahimoth, Elkanah his son, Zophai his son," which matches the pattern of the list and the parallel in 6:35. Many translations follow it. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as it does throughout, which leaves the verse a little rough.

p: The Hebrew list ends with Elkanah, Samuel's father. The Greek adds "Samuel his son."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, BSB
Greek (some manuscripts), as reported in commentaries; NIV
readings.orig: Ελκανα υἱὸς αὐτοῦ, Σαμουηλ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: Elkanah his son, Samuel his son
readings.plain: Elkanah his son, Samuel his son.

why: The next verse begins "the sons of Samuel," so Samuel's name is needed somewhere, and the parallel list in 6:33–34 includes him. A scribe could easily have skipped it. But the Hebrew can be understood as it stands, since every reader knew Elkanah's son, and the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: the firstborn, Joel, and the second, Abijah
p: The Hebrew reads "the firstborn, Vashni, and Abijah." Vashni looks like "and the second." Joel is Samuel's firstborn in 1 Samuel 8:2.

readings.w: Lucianic Greek and the Syriac, as reported in commentaries; 6:33; 1 Samuel 8:2; NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: the firstborn, Joel, and the second, Abijah
readings.plain: the firstborn, Joel, and the second, Abijah

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV

why: This is the one place in these chapters where the Plain English Translation does not follow the Leningrad Codex (read with its Qere notes). Vashni is not a name found anywhere else; read as ve-hasheni, it means "and the second." So the Hebrew lost the name Joel after "the firstborn" and turned "the second" into a name. 1 Samuel 8:2 says, "His oldest son's name was Joel, and his second son's name was Abijah," and 6:33 calls Heman "son of Joel, son of Samuel." The evidence is strong enough to restore Joel.

p: The Leningrad Codex reads Hilez. Printed Hebrew Bibles read Hilen, and Joshua 21:15 has Holon.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
Other Masoretic manuscripts and the printed Rabbinic Bible, as reported in commentaries; KJV, BSB
Joshua 21:15

why: The final letters zayin and nun are easily confused, and Hilen is closer to Joshua's Holon, so Hilez is probably a slip. The Plain English Translation still prints the Leningrad Codex as it stands, as it does for Diphath (1:6); all three names refer to the same town (Joshua 15:51).

a: Ashan with its pastureland and Beth-shemesh with its pastureland.
p: Joshua 21:16 lists Ain, Juttah and Beth-shemesh. Chronicles has Ashan and Beth-shemesh, and no Juttah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
readings.en: and Ashan with its pastureland and Beth-shemesh
readings.plain: Ashan with its pastureland and Beth-shemesh with its pastureland.

readings.w: Syriac and Joshua 21:16, as reported in commentaries; NIV, BSB
readings.plain: Ashan with its pastureland, Juttah with its pastureland and Beth-shemesh with its pastureland.

why: Joshua's list gives nine towns from Judah and Simeon and four from Benjamin, thirteen in all, the total Chronicles also gives (6:60). Chronicles lists only eleven names, so Juttah (and Gibeon, 6:60) probably dropped out. Ashan here stands where Joshua has Ain, perhaps a different reading of the same town. Many translations add Juttah. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic list and lets the note explain.

a: From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Geba
p: Joshua 21:17 has Gibeon and Geba from Benjamin. Chronicles names Geba but not Gibeon.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: and from the tribe of Benjamin: Geba
readings.plain: From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Geba

readings.w: Joshua 21:17, followed by NIV, BSB
readings.plain: From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Gibeon with its pastureland, Geba

why: Without Gibeon the count "thirteen towns" does not work. A scribe could easily skip from Gibeon to Geba, which look alike in Hebrew. Gibeon matters to Chronicles (the tabernacle stood there, 16:39), so its absence is surely an accident. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic Text and notes the gap.

a: Rimmono with its pastureland and Tabor with its pastureland
t: Two towns of Zebulun, or four?
p: The Hebrew gives two towns from Zebulun. Joshua 21:34–35 gives four: Jokneam, Kartah, Dimnah and Nahalal.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, BSB
readings.en: Rimmono with its pastureland, Tabor with its pastureland
readings.plain: Rimmono with its pastureland and Tabor with its pastureland

readings.w: Some Greek manuscripts, as reported in commentaries, and Joshua 21:34; NIV
readings.plain: Jokneam with its pastureland, Kartah with its pastureland, Rimmono with its pastureland and Tabor with its pastureland

why: The Merarites received twelve towns (6:63). Chronicles names only ten, so two are missing, and the Greek supplies Jokneam and Kartah from Joshua. Rimmono and Tabor may be Chronicles' names for Dimnah and Nahalal, or different towns of a later time. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.

p: The Leningrad Codex reads Ayyah, an unknown town. Many Hebrew manuscripts and early printed Bibles read Gaza.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); NIV, ESV, BSB
Many Hebrew manuscripts and the early printed Rabbinic Bibles; KJV

why: Gaza, on the Philistine coast, is far outside Ephraim's land, so the reading is very unlikely in a list of Ephraim's towns. Ayyah may be Ai near Bethel (Hebrew Ai and Ayyah are related forms; compare Aija in Nehemiah 11:31). The letters yod and zayin look alike, which explains the confusion.

p: The reading tradition (Qere) has Birzaith, the written consonants (Ketiv) Birzoth. KJV blends them as Birzavith.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); NIV, ESV, BSB
Ketiv (the written consonants)
KJV (Ketiv consonants with Qere vowels)

why: Birzaith is probably a town: "father of" in these lists often means founder (see 2:42). A village called Bir Zeit, north of Jerusalem, may preserve the name.

t: Rohgah and Hubbah, or Rohagah and Jachbah?
p: The written consonants (Ketiv) have Rohagah and Jachbah. The reading tradition (Qere) has Rohgah and Hubbah.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); NIV, ESV, BSB
Ketiv (the written consonants)
KJV (Ketiv consonants for the second name, with Qere vowels)

why: Both pairs are spelling differences in otherwise unknown names. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as it does throughout.

a: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon
p: 9:35 names "the father of Gibeon, Jeiel." 8:29 has no name. Most translations add Jeiel here from 9:35.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: in Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon
readings.plain: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon

readings.w: Some Greek manuscripts, as reported in commentaries, and 9:35; NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.plain: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel

why: The two copies of Saul's family (8:29–38; 9:35–44) help restore each other. Jeiel was probably lost here by accident. The Plain English Translation keeps each copy as it stands, so the difference stays visible. See the note on 9:35.

p: 9:36 lists Ner among the sons of the father of Gibeon; 8:30 does not. Ner is needed for 8:33.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, BSB
readings.en: and Kish and Baal and Nadab

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (Greek), as reported in commentaries, and 9:36; NIV, ESV
readings.en: and Kish and Baal and Ner and Nadab

why: Ner fathered Kish (8:33), so the list ought to name him. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. Mikloth too is missing from 8:31, though 8:32 begins with him.

a: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan
p: The Hebrew names six sons including Bocheru. The Greek reads "his firstborn" and adds Asa at the end, so it also has six.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.orig: עַזְרִיקָם בֹּכְרוּ וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל וּשְׁעַרְיָה וְעֹבַדְיָה וְחָנָן
readings.en: Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan
readings.plain: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan

readings.w: Greek (Brenton's text)
readings.orig: Εζρικαμ πρωτότοκος αὐτοῦ, καὶ Ισμαηλ, καὶ Σαρια, καὶ Αβδια, καὶ Αναν, καὶ Ασα
readings.en: Ezricam his firstborn, and Ismael, and Saraia, and Abdia, and Anan, and Asa
readings.plain: Azrikam his firstborn, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, Hanan and Asa

why: The Hebrew consonants bkrw can be read as the name Bocheru or as bekhoro, "his firstborn," and the Greek fits the pattern of 8:39 ("Ulam his firstborn"). With Bocheru gone, the Greek keeps the count of six by adding Asa, which may have arisen from a repetition of the letters of Azel. Both readings are possible. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowels, which are the same in 9:44.

p: The reading tradition (Qere) has Jeiel, matching 8:29's missing name. The written consonants (Ketiv) have Jeuel.

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretic reading tradition); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB
Ketiv (the written consonants)

why: A yod/waw difference, common in names. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere.

p: 8:35 lists four sons of Micah, ending with Ahaz. 9:41 lists three, though 9:42 begins "Ahaz fathered..."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (the KJV supplies "and Ahaz" in italics)
Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Greek, Syriac and Latin Vulgate, as reported in commentaries, and 8:35; NIV, ESV, BSB
readings.en: and Melech and Tahrea and Ahaz

why: Ahaz is surely original here, as 8:35 and 9:42 show. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew as it stands, as it does with the other gaps in the two copies of this list; the note on 9:35 compares them. Tahrea here is Tarea in 8:35.
